text: Johnson had no wish to praise Shakespeare by the measure of his own age, and he distrusted the praise that any single age bestows. Fashion admires what flatters it, and one generation may be pleased with a writer for reasons the next will think trivial or will not understand at all. The only test he would allow was duration. A work that has been read and valued through many changes of manners and opinion must owe its hold to something more than the accident of its first reception. By this test, he held, Shakespeare's case was already decided. He had been dead a century and a half; the language had altered, the stage had altered, and the taste of critics had swung from one doctrine to another. Still the plays were acted, read, and quoted by men who knew nothing of the circumstances that first produced them. Johnson put the matter in a figure of his own: "The stream of time, which is continually washing the dissoluble fabricks of other poets, passes without injury by the adamant of Shakespeare." (Johnson 1765) The poets who had shared his stage had worn away in that stream; Shakespeare had not.
